channel.title: The Discovery Wire
channel.description: Science, decoded — the experiments, the instruments, and the questions nobody has answered yet.

item.title: Recall Radar: Why the Pantry Needs a System, Not a Junk Drawer
item.description: Food recalls are announced every week, and almost none of them reach the kitchens they apply to. The gap isn't awareness — it's that nobody has a list of what's actually in their pantry to check against.

item.title: One Month of Dinners, Decided Once
item.description: "What's for dinner?" is not a cooking problem — it's a decision problem, and it gets asked 30 times a month. The rotation system that answers it once, and why the structure matters more than the recipes.

item.title: The 2 A.M. Test: What Your Household Needs Within Arm's Reach
item.description: Emergencies don't schedule themselves for a calm Saturday afternoon. The real question is whether the information your household needs exists in one known place when it's dark, loud, and urgent.

item.title: Running a Mystery Game Night That Actually Works
item.description: The difference between a mystery night people talk about for a month and one that fizzles by the second drink is almost never the mystery. It's the hosting. Here's the structure that works.

item.title: How a Print-and-Play Cold Case Actually Works
item.description: No actors, no game master, no app — just a folder of evidence and a table of people who think they can read it better than the detective did. Inside the mechanics of the case-file mystery.

item.title: GTA VI Is Already Out in New Zealand — How Tonight's Global Rollout Actually Works
item.description: Rockstar is launching Grand Theft Auto VI the slow way: midnight, one country at a time. New Zealand started playing at 6 AM Eastern today, and the wave reaches the United States at midnight Eastern tonight. Here is how the rollout moves, hour by hour.

item.title: That GTA VI Box on the Shelf Has No Disc In It — Read This Before You Buy
item.description: The physical edition of Grand Theft Auto VI is a download code in a box — there is no disc. For disc-console owners, collectors, and anyone gift-wrapping a copy this week, that changes what you are actually buying, and why the code should be redeemed today, not tonight.

item.title: GTA VI Editions Compared: $79.99, $99.99, a $20 Upgrade — and a $399.99 Box With No Game In It
item.description: Grand Theft Auto VI sells in exactly two editions, plus an upgrade path and one very expensive merchandise box that does not include the game at all. Every verified US price, what each tier actually adds, and who each one is for.

item.title: Two Monster Black Holes Were Already Shining in One Galaxy Less Than a Billion Years After the Big Bang
item.description: Astronomers found the most distant compact quasar pair ever identified — two actively feeding supermassive black holes, about 1.5 billion and 400 million solar masses, separated by roughly 18,100 light-years in a galaxy seen just 900 million years after the Big Bang.

item.title: Earthquake Watch: The Week's Biggest Quake Was Felt by 10 People — a Tiny Utah Quake Was Felt by 383
item.description: The public USGS-tracked feeds for the week ending Nov 16, 2026: 296 quakes of magnitude 2.5 or greater, one M6.6 off Indonesia that almost nobody felt, and a magnitude 3.4 near Enterprise, Utah that 383 people reported. Roundup only — never predictions.

item.title: The Magnetic Tiles That Started It All: Magna-Tiles Classic 32-Piece
item.description: Every December the same question arrives from parents of preschoolers: which building toy actually survives childhood? The Magna-Tiles Classic 32-piece set has been answering it since 2005. Here's what it actually is, and what it isn't.

item.title: The Step Up From Binoculars: Celestron AstroMaster 70AZ, Honestly
item.description: Our binoculars guide ends with "telescope later." For readers who are at "later," the AstroMaster 70AZ is the budget refractor that has held the beginner slot for years. Here's what it actually is, and what it isn't.

item.title: Giant Binoculars, Honest Verdict: The Celestron SkyMaster 15x70
item.description: Readers ask what gear we'd point at the night sky first. Our answer hasn't changed in years: a big pair of astronomy binoculars — and the SkyMaster 15x70 is the budget classic. Here's what it actually is, and what it isn't.

item.title: Snap Circuits Jr. SC-100: The STEM Kit That Teaches Real Circuits
item.description: Most "electronics kits for kids" are plastic toys with a battery hidden inside. Elenco's Snap Circuits Jr. is the real thing — actual switches, motors, and speakers that snap into working circuits. A gear guide for the young experimenters in the house.

item.title: Something Invisible Is Orbiting a Red Giant — and It May Be Too Heavy to Exist
item.description: Astronomers have found a red giant with an unseen companion in the system J0008+0128. The invisible object weighs an estimated 1.8 to 2.8 Suns — right in the puzzling mass gap between the heaviest neutron stars and the lightest black holes.

item.title: Euclid Just Handed Us the First Draft of the Universe's 3D Map
item.description: The Euclid Consortium and ESA have released DR1 Foundation — 13 months of observations covering a patch of sky equal to 9,500 full moons, with light from more than a billion objects. It is the foundation for the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, built to attack the dark universe: dark matter, dark energy, and why the expansion of the universe is accelerating.

item.title: Webb's Little Red Dots May Be Black Holes Being Born
item.description: Since the James Webb Space Telescope opened its eye, astronomers have been puzzled by hundreds of tiny red specks in the early universe that no theory predicted. New simulations from a University of Portsmouth-led team say they may be primeval galaxies where the first supermassive black holes are forming by direct collapse — a model that fits, not a sighting.

item.title: The Disappearing Planet: A Hidden Neighbor Is Tilting TOI-2535 b Out of View
item.description: For seven years, NASA's TESS watched a hot Jupiter called TOI-2535 b cross its star every 8.25 days. Then the transits got shorter, shallower, and late — and in 2026 they stopped. A UCLA-led team says an unseen neighbor is wobbling its orbit like a top.

item.title: The Supernova Impostor: Chandra Finds What Keeps Making a Giant Star Erupt Every 113 Days
item.description: AT 2016blu in NGC 4559 has erupted at least 27 times since 2012 without destroying itself. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory caught it mid-outburst in March 2026 — and found a hidden black hole or neutron star companion pulling material off it every 113 days.

item.title: Hera Just Saw the Side of Didymos DART Never Photographed
item.description: ESA's Hera spacecraft returned its first close-range image of the Didymos asteroid system on November 5, 2026 — a boulder-strewn face of Didymos that DART's camera never saw, with Dimorphos peeking from shadow.
